Renzo Piano. The Italian architect known for high-tech, transparent designs that celebrate structure and materials, balancing technological innovation with poetic sensibility and earning him the Pritzker Prize.

Piano was born in 1937. He co-designed the Pompidou Centre in Paris with Richard Rogers in 1977, a radical high-tech building with exposed structural and mechanical systems painted in bright colors, turning the building's innards outward. He designed the Kansai International Airport in Osaka in 1994, a massive lightweight steel and glass structure floating over reclaimed land, achieving both technical and aesthetic grace.

He created the Menil Collection in Houston in 1986, a transparent glass and steel museum that honors both contemporary art and the surrounding residential neighborhood through refined minimalism. He pioneered high-tech architecture by celebrating materials, structure, and mechanical systems as aesthetic elements rather than hiding them behind facades.

Piano studied engineering and apprenticed with Gio Ponti, learning to integrate craft sensibility with industrial production. He designed the Paul Klee Centre in Bern in 2002, using undulating wood and glass forms that respond to the landscape while housing one of the world's greatest art collections. He is known for using advanced materials including titanium and carbon fiber along with computer modeling, while maintaining human scale and site-specific response.

He worked closely with Richard Rogers on the Pompidou Centre, and both championed high-tech transparency and structural honesty. Piano is a defining practitioner of high-tech architecture, and his work defines the aesthetic possibilities of the movement. While Frank Gehry explores digital form, Piano emphasizes structural clarity over sculptural expressionism, creating a distinct voice within contemporary design.
